fixed.q: Which software is used for the management, maintenance and retrieval of data stored in a database?
fixed.w: A DBMS stores, retrieves and manages data safely with integrity and concurrent access.

fixed.q: Which of the following is a problem of file systems that a DBMS solves with transactions?
fixed.w: File-system problems: redundancy and inconsistency, data isolation, integrity problems, atomicity problems, concurrent-access anomalies, security.

fixed.q: Which level of data abstraction describes HOW data is actually stored (files, indexes)?
fixed.w: Three-schema (ANSI/SPARC): physical = how stored; logical = what is stored (tables, relationships); view = the part a user group sees.

fixed.q: A logical schema in a database:
o: Is the standard way of organising information into accessible parts
Describes how data is actually stored on disk
fixed.w: Logical (conceptual) schema = what data is stored and how it relates. How it is stored on disk = physical schema.

fixed.q: Changing the internal (physical) schema without changing the conceptual schema is called:
fixed.w: Physical independence is easier to achieve. Logical independence = change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas/applications (harder).

fixed.q: The data in a database at a particular moment is called the:
fixed.w: Schema = overall design (rarely changes); instance = snapshot of data (changes often).

fixed.q: The information stored in the catalog (data dictionary) of a database is called:
fixed.w: Metadata = data about data (table structures, constraints).

fixed.q: Which of these is NOT a function of the DBA?
fixed.w: DBA: schema definition, storage structure and access methods, schema modification, granting authorisation, integrity constraints, routine maintenance.

fixed.q: In DBMS architecture, which component converts DDL statements into metadata tables in the data dictionary?
fixed.w: Query processor: DDL interpreter, DML compiler, embedded DML pre-compiler, query optimizer. Storage manager: authorization, integrity, transaction, file, buffer managers.

fixed.q: Which of these are steps in query processing?
o: Parsing and translation, optimisation, and evaluation
fixed.w: Query processing = parsing & translation → optimisation → evaluation.

fixed.q: A relational-algebra operation annotated with instructions on how to evaluate it is called an:
fixed.w: A sequence of evaluation primitives forms a query-evaluation plan.

fixed.q: Communication between an application program and a database server occurs through:
fixed.w: ODBC/JDBC are database-connectivity APIs.

fixed.q: Which DBMS is developed by Microsoft?
Which of the following is NOT an approach to database design?
fixed.w: Approaches: top-down, bottom-up, inside-out, mixed.

fixed.q: Which language is referred to as a database language?
A deductive database is one that:
o: Uses logic programming (e.g. Datalog) to derive information
fixed.w: Multimedia = images/audio/video; temporal = changes over time; GIS = spatial data.

fixed.q: The ER model was proposed by:
fixed.w: Codd proposed the relational model (1970); Armstrong's axioms (1974).

fixed.q: In an ER diagram, an entity set, an attribute and a relationship set are drawn respectively as:
fixed.w: Double ellipse = multivalued, dashed ellipse = derived, underlined = key attribute.

fixed.q: Which ER notation shows a weak entity set?
fixed.w: Its identifying relationship is a double diamond; its discriminator (partial key) has a dashed underline.

fixed.q: The primary key of a weak entity set is:
o: The owner's primary key plus the weak entity's discriminator
It has no key at all
fixed.w: A weak entity is existence-dependent on its owner; its participation in the identifying relationship is always total.

fixed.q: A multivalued attribute (e.g. several phone numbers) is drawn as:
fixed.w: In tables a multivalued attribute becomes a separate table: owner PK + attribute, together as PK.

fixed.q: Age computed from Date of Birth is an example of a:
fixed.w: Composite = divisible into parts (Name → first, last).

fixed.q: Descriptive attributes are used to record information about:
fixed.w: An attribute attached to a relationship diamond (e.g. 'since' on works-for).

fixed.q: An association among several entities is called a:
In ER diagrams, total participation is shown by:
fixed.w: Total = every entity takes part (every loan must belong to a customer). Arrow points to the 'one' side.

fixed.q: An employee supervises another employee. This relationship is:
fixed.w: Degree = number of entity sets taking part. Binary is the most common.

fixed.q: When converting ER to tables, an M:N binary relationship needs:
o: A separate table with both primary keys as foreign keys
No table; put a foreign key on the N side
fixed.w: 1:N → FK on the N side (no new table). 1:1 → FK on either side (prefer total participation). Minimum tables: M:N = 3, 1:N = 2.

fixed.q: Which ER relationship type corresponds to a foreign key (not a separate relation) in the relational model?
fixed.w: M:N needs a separate relationship relation.

fixed.q: Combining lower-level entity sets into a higher-level entity set based on common features (bottom-up) is:
fixed.w: Specialization is top-down (ISA). Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity so it can take part in another relationship.

fixed.q: Which are types of connection trap in the ER model? I. Fan trap II. Chasm trap
fixed.w: Fan trap = ambiguous path fanning out; chasm trap = missing path due to partial participation.

fixed.q: The modality of a relationship with no explicit need to occur (optional) is:
fixed.w: Modality = minimum participation: 0 optional, 1 mandatory.

fixed.q: A collection of entities that have the same attributes is called (Elmasri's terms) an:
fixed.w: Entity set = the entities of a type at a given moment. The 2024 key chose 'Entity type'.

fixed.q: The values of the attributes in a database describe a particular:
The relational model was proposed by:
fixed.w: Codd also gave 12 rules for a true RDBMS (numbered 0–12, so 13 with rule zero; exam answer 12).

fixed.q: How many rules did Dr E. F. Codd give to qualify a database as an RDBMS?
What is the cardinality of a relation with 500 tuples and 50 attributes?
fixed.w: Cardinality = number of rows (tuples). Degree (arity) = number of columns.

fixed.q: What makes a database a relational database?
Which is NOT a property of a relational table?
o: Each column has a unique name
fixed.w: Order of rows and columns doesn't matter.

fixed.q: A minimal super key (no proper subset is a super key) is a:
fixed.w: Primary key = the candidate key chosen by the DBA (no NULLs, one per table); others are alternate keys.

fixed.q: A relation may have more than one key. Each of these is called a:
Which attribute is most suitable as a primary key?
fixed.w: It must be unique and non-null.

fixed.q: An attribute is a foreign key if the ___ key of one relation is used as an attribute in another relation.
Relation r1 includes the primary key of relation r2 as an attribute. r1 is called the:
fixed.w: r2 (whose PK is referenced) is the referenced relation.

fixed.q: A referential integrity constraint is specified with the help of a:
fixed.w: An FK value must match an existing PK value or be NULL.

fixed.q: Which integrity constraint is specified between two relations to keep their tuples consistent?
fixed.w: Entity integrity = PK cannot be NULL.

fixed.q: Domain constraints, functional dependencies and referential integrity are special forms of a(n):
fixed.w: CREATE ASSERTION expresses any general constraint.

fixed.q: An attribute that is a member of at least one candidate key is a:
fixed.w: Used in 2NF/3NF definitions.

fixed.q: Entity integrity says that:
o: A primary-key attribute cannot be NULL
A foreign key must be NULL
Every table must have a foreign key

fixed.q: Which anomaly occurs when deleting the last student of a branch also deletes the branch's details?
fixed.w: Insertion: can't add a branch until a student joins. Update: changing the HOD needs many rows changed.

fixed.q: Anomalies are avoided by splitting the offending relation into multiple relations. This is called:
'An attribute of a table cannot hold multiple values' is the property of:
fixed.w: 1NF: atomic values, no multivalued or composite attributes.

fixed.q: Which normal form disallows relations within relations (relations as attribute values)?
A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and:
o: No non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key
Every determinant is a super key
fixed.w: Partial dependency: prime part of a key → non-prime. A relation whose candidate keys are all single attributes is automatically in 2NF.

fixed.q: 3NF requires that for every non-trivial FD α → β:
o: α is a super key OR β is a prime attribute
fixed.w: BCNF drops the 'β prime' exception: α must be a super key.

fixed.q: Which statement is true?
o: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF
A relation where all attributes are prime is always in BCNF
fixed.w: All attributes prime → always 3NF but maybe not BCNF. BCNF decomposition is lossless but may not preserve dependencies.

fixed.q: 4NF removes:
fixed.w: 5NF (PJNF) removes join dependencies not implied by keys.

fixed.q: Decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if:
o: R1 ∩ R2 is a super key of R1 or of R2 (and R1 ∪ R2 = R)
R1 and R2 have the same number of attributes
fixed.w: A lossy decomposition produces spurious tuples on joining. Lossless is mandatory; dependency preservation is desirable.

fixed.q: Which decomposition property can always be achieved together with losslessness in 3NF, but not always in BCNF?
An FD α → β is trivial when:
fixed.w: e.g. AB → A. Completely non-trivial: α ∩ β = ∅.

fixed.q: Which is NOT one of Armstrong's three primary axioms?
fixed.w: Union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity and composition are derived rules. The 2023 PYQ keyed pseudo-transitivity as the one that doesn't really follow Armstrong's axioms.

fixed.q: If X → Y and WY → Z, then WX → Z by:
fixed.w: Union: X→Y, X→Z ⇒ X→YZ. Decomposition: X→YZ ⇒ X→Y.

fixed.q: R(PQRSTU), F = {P → RT, Q → S, R → PS, QS → TU}. The closure of PQ is:
fixed.w: PQ → R, T (from P), S (from Q), then QS → TU gives U. All six attributes.

fixed.q: R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}. Which is NOT a candidate key?
fixed.w: A⁺ = ABCDE, E⁺ = all, BC⁺ = BCDEA. B⁺ = BD only.

fixed.q: Instance A B C = (1,2,3), (4,2,3), (5,3,3). Which FD does NOT hold?
fixed.w: BC = (2,3) occurs with A = 1 and A = 4.

fixed.q: Two FD sets F and G are equivalent if:
o: They have the same number of FDs
fixed.w: A canonical (minimal) cover is equivalent to F with single-attribute RHS, no extraneous LHS attributes, no redundant FDs.

fixed.q: When data is frequently added to or deleted from a file, its volatility is:
Sequential file organisation: I. The entire file must be read for insertion/deletion. II. On average, half the records are processed to find one. Which is correct?
DASD stands for:
In an ordered file of n blocks, binary search on the ordering key needs about how many block accesses?
fixed.w: Unordered (heap) file needs linear search: n/2 on average.

fixed.q: A ___ index is an ordered file of fixed-length records with two fields: the primary key and a pointer to a disk block.
fixed.w: Primary index: one entry per block (anchor record), sparse.

fixed.q: A secondary index (on an attribute the file isn't ordered by) is:
fixed.w: Clustering index: file ordered on a non-key attribute, one entry per distinct value. A file can have at most one primary/clustering index but many secondary ones.

fixed.q: Which statement about a clustered index is true?
o: It is created by default on a unique (primary) key column
It is not associated with a table
It is never created on a unique key column
A table can have many clustered indexes
fixed.w: Rows are physically sorted by it, so one per table (SQL Server default on the PRIMARY KEY).

fixed.q: What is true about indexes?
o: Indexes with large keys make the SQL Server engine work harder
Indexes improve performance even with very frequent updates
fixed.w: Large keys → fewer entries per page; frequent updates also slow down because indexes must be maintained.

fixed.q: An index that contains every column a query needs, so no further lookup into the table is required, is a:
In an RDBMS, B+ trees are preferred to binary trees because:
o: Disk access is much slower than memory access, and B+ trees need few disk accesses
Disks are more reliable than memory
fixed.w: High fan-out → short tree → few block reads. (Key option: 'memory access is faster than disk access'.)

fixed.q: In a B+ tree:
o: All record pointers are in the leaves, and leaves are linked for range queries
Data pointers are stored in every node
fixed.w: B-tree stores data pointers in every node. Both are balanced: all leaves at the same level.

fixed.q: In a B-tree of order m, a non-root internal node has at least how many children?
fixed.w: Max m children and m − 1 keys; root has at least 2 children (unless a leaf).

fixed.q: Hashing as a file organisation is best for:
fixed.w: Collisions: chaining or open addressing.

fixed.q: Relational algebra is ___ while relational calculus is ___.
fixed.w: RA says what and how; RC says only what. Safe RC = RA in power (relationally complete).

fixed.q: Which is NOT one of the six fundamental relational-algebra operators?
fixed.w: Fundamental: select σ, project π, rename ρ, union ∪, set difference −, Cartesian product ×. Join, intersection, division are derived.

fixed.q: The select (σ) and project (π) operators pick, respectively:
fixed.w: π removes duplicates (relational algebra is set-based).

fixed.q: Which operation gives all tuples that are in R but not in S?
What does STUDENT × COURSE compute?
fixed.w: m tuples × n tuples → m·n tuples; degree adds up.

fixed.q: Union, intersection and difference need the relations to be:
o: Union-compatible: same arity and same domains column by column

fixed.q: Which operator answers 'students who completed ALL tasks'?
fixed.w: R ÷ S = π_X(R) − π_X((π_X(R) × S) − R).

fixed.q: A natural join of two relations with no common attributes gives:
Which join keeps all tuples of the left relation, filling NULLs where there is no match?
fixed.w: Full outer join keeps all tuples of both.

fixed.q: R(P, Q, R1, R2, R3), S(P, Q, S1, S2), key {P, Q} for both. Which are equivalent? (I) π_P(R ⋈ S) (II) π_P(R) ⋈ π_P(S) (III) π_P(π_PQ(R) ∩ π_PQ(S)) (IV) π_P(π_PQ(R) − (π_PQ(R) − π_PQ(S)))
fixed.w: R − (R − S) = R ∩ S. (II) joins only on P, so it can match different Q values.

fixed.q: In tuple relational calculus, a query has the form:
fixed.w: DRC uses domain variables {⟨x1…xn⟩ | COND}. Unsafe expressions (infinite results) are not allowed.

fixed.q: SQL was first developed by IBM for System R under the name:
fixed.w: Structured English Query Language; standardised by ANSI/ISO as SQL-86.

fixed.q: Which is used to define the structure of a relation as well as delete relations?
fixed.w: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME.

fixed.q: What type of statement is: insert into instructor values (10211, 'Smith', 'Biology', 66000);
fixed.w: DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (and SELECT).

fixed.q: Which is NOT a data manipulation command?
fixed.w: CREATE is DDL.

fixed.q: GRANT and REVOKE belong to:
fixed.w: TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT (some books put these under DCL).

fixed.q: Which command makes permanent all changes made since the start of a transaction?
fixed.w: ROLLBACK undoes them; SAVEPOINT marks a point to roll back to.

fixed.q: Which statement is true about DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
o: DELETE can use WHERE and be rolled back; TRUNCATE removes all rows keeping the table; DROP removes the table
fixed.w: TRUNCATE and DROP are DDL.

fixed.q: Which symbol with SELECT retrieves all attribute values of the selected tuples?
The ___ clause retains only one copy of identical tuples.
fixed.w: SQL keeps duplicates by default (ALL).

fixed.q: By default, ORDER BY lists items in ___ order.
Which operator in a WHERE clause matches a character pattern?
fixed.w: % = any number of characters (0 or more), _ = exactly one character.

fixed.q: WHERE name LIKE '_a%' matches names that:
fixed.w: _ is exactly one character, % is any substring.

fixed.q: Which is NOT an aggregate function in SQL?
fixed.w: The five aggregates: AVG, MIN, MAX, SUM, COUNT. (Union, intersect, minus are set operators.)

fixed.q: Which aggregate does NOT ignore NULL values?
fixed.w: All aggregates skip NULLs except COUNT(*), which counts rows.

fixed.q: WHERE filters ___ while HAVING filters ___.
o: rows before grouping; groups after grouping
rows after grouping; rows before grouping
fixed.w: Aggregates are allowed in HAVING, not in WHERE. Order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY.

fixed.q: The standard SQL concatenation operator is:
fixed.w: SQL Server uses +, MySQL CONCAT().

fixed.q: The '< ALL' comparison with a subquery means:
o: Less than the minimum value in the subquery
fixed.w: > ALL = above the max; < ANY = below the max; = ANY = IN.

fixed.q: Which SQL operator tests whether any of the subquery values meets the condition?
EMPLOYEE has 10 rows and a non-NULL UNIQUE SALARY. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE SALARY > ALL (SELECT SALARY FROM EMPLOYEE); prints:
fixed.w: No salary can be greater than itself.

fixed.q: With no parentheses, NOT, AND, OR in SQL are evaluated in the order:
The DEFAULT constraint:
o: Provides a value for a column when none is specified
Ensures a column cannot be NULL
fixed.w: NOT NULL, CHECK and UNIQUE do the other three. UNIQUE allows NULL; PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL.

fixed.q: Which statement about CHAR(n) and VARCHAR(n) is true?
o: CHAR(n) is fixed-length; VARCHAR(n) is variable-length
CHAR(n) is variable-length; VARCHAR(n) is fixed-length

fixed.q: Which is NOT an SQL data type?
To drop a constraint from a table, we use:
o: ALTER TABLE with a DROP clause
fixed.w: ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT c;

fixed.q: DROP SCHEMA s RESTRICT:
o: Drops the schema only if it has no elements
Drops the schema and everything in it
fixed.w: CASCADE drops it with all its contents.

fixed.q: Which SQL function returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to a number?
Which SQL Server function returns the current database-system timestamp as a datetime value (no time-zone offset)?
fixed.w: MySQL: NOW(), CURDATE().

fixed.q: DATEDIFF: I. Reports the difference between startdate and enddate. II. Its datepart can be given in a variable. Which is correct?
fixed.w: datepart must be a literal keyword (year, month, day…), not a variable.

fixed.q: The syntax INSERT INTO table (cols) VALUES (values); lets you:
o: Insert one row at a time
Insert one column at a time
Insert multiple columns at a time only
fixed.w: (Many DBMSs also allow several VALUES lists, but this syntax as given inserts one row.)

fixed.q: Given R(w, x) and S(y, z), SELECT DISTINCT w, x FROM R, S equals R if:
o: R has no duplicates and S is non-empty
R and S have no duplicates
S has no duplicates and R is non-empty
R and S have the same number of tuples
fixed.w: An empty S makes the product empty.

fixed.q: To retrieve data from a table in PostgreSQL, we use:
fixed.w: \dt lists tables in psql.

fixed.q: Trigger code is written in (as per the key):
fixed.w: A trigger runs automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (Event–Condition–Action).

fixed.q: A view in SQL is:
o: A virtual table defined by a query, not stored
A copy of a table stored on disk
fixed.w: Materialised views are stored.

fixed.q: SQL statements built and executed at run time from user input are:
fixed.w: Embedded SQL is fixed at compile time. A cursor processes a result one row at a time.

fixed.q: Which ACID property is ensured by the concurrency-control manager?
fixed.w: Atomicity and durability: recovery manager (undo/redo with log). Consistency: programmer/constraints.

fixed.q: 'Changes of a committed transaction persist even after a system failure' is:
After executing its last statement, a transaction enters the ___ state.
fixed.w: Active → partially committed → committed; failed → aborted (then restart or kill).

fixed.q: Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item, and:
o: At least one is a write
fixed.w: Read–read never conflicts.

fixed.q: A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph:
fixed.w: Edge Ti → Tj for each conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes first. A topological order gives the equivalent serial schedule.

fixed.q: S1: R1(A); R1(B); R2(A); R2(B); W2(B); W1(A). S2: R1(A); R2(A); R2(B); W2(B); R1(B); W1(A). Which is conflict serializable?
fixed.w: S1: R1(B) before W2(B) → T1→T2; R2(A) before W1(A) → T2→T1: cycle. S2: W2(B) before R1(B) and R2(A) before W1(A) → only T2→T1.

fixed.q: Which statement is true?
o: Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable
Every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable
View serializability is tested with a precedence graph in linear time
fixed.w: View-but-not-conflict serializable schedules contain blind writes; testing view serializability is NP-complete.

fixed.q: Which scenario may lead to an irrecoverable schedule?
o: A transaction reads an item written by an uncommitted transaction (and commits first)
A transaction reads after another uncommitted read
A transaction reads an item written by a committed transaction
A transaction writes after an uncommitted read
fixed.w: Recoverable: the writer commits before the reader commits. Cascadeless: no reads of uncommitted data.

fixed.q: A schedule in which a transaction reads only committed data (avoiding cascading rollbacks) is:
fixed.w: strict ⊆ cascadeless ⊆ recoverable.

fixed.q: Transaction A holds a shared lock on R. If B requests a shared lock on R, it will:
fixed.w: S–S compatible; S–X, X–S, X–X are not.

fixed.q: Two-phase locking guarantees:
o: Conflict serializability (but not freedom from deadlock)
fixed.w: Growing phase (acquire only) then shrinking phase (release only); serial order = order of lock points.

fixed.q: Which 2PL variant holds all exclusive locks until commit, giving recoverable and cascadeless schedules?
fixed.w: Rigorous 2PL holds all locks (S and X) until commit. Conservative 2PL acquires all locks before starting and is deadlock-free.

fixed.q: Ti requesting an item held by Tj may wait only if Ti is older; otherwise Ti is rolled back. This is:
fixed.w: Wound-wait: an older requester wounds (aborts) the younger holder; a younger requester waits.

fixed.q: Deadlock among transactions is detected with a:
fixed.w: A cycle in the wait-for graph = deadlock. (The 2017 SSC key printed option A; the standard answer is wait-for graph.)

fixed.q: In timestamp ordering, if Ti issues read(Q) and TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q):
o: The read is rejected and Ti is rolled back
fixed.w: Timestamp ordering is conflict serializable and deadlock-free (no waiting) but can starve.

fixed.q: The Thomas write rule:
o: Ignores an obsolete write instead of rolling the transaction back
fixed.w: It allows some view-serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

fixed.q: Under deferred database modification, recovery needs:
fixed.w: Immediate modification needs undo and redo. Write-ahead logging: the log record is written before the database is changed.

fixed.q: Shadow paging:
o: Keeps a shadow page table and switches to the new table atomically on commit
Needs both undo and redo logs
Copies every page at transaction start
fixed.w: Failure before commit → discard the current table. Downsides: fragmentation, garbage collection.

fixed.q: Checkpoints in log-based recovery:
o: Limit how much of the log must be scanned after a crash
fixed.w: Committed after the checkpoint → redo; incomplete → undo.

fixed.q: In SQL, which of the following is correct command for schema evolution, if the RESTRICT option is chosen than the schema is dropped only if schema has no element in it?
fixed.w: DROP SCHEMA name RESTRICT drops the schema only if it contains no elements; CASCADE drops everything.

fixed.q: Which of the following is an Aggregate operator in Structured Query Language?
fixed.w: COUNT is an aggregate function; UNION, INTERSECT and MINUS are set operators.

fixed.q: Which of the following statements is true?
o: The basic data type char(n) is a fixed-length character string and varchar(n) is a variable-length character string.
The basic data type char(n) is a fixed-length character string and varchar(n) is an equal-length character string.
The basic data type char(n) is an equal-length character string and varchar(n) is a variable-length character string.
The basic data type char(n) is a variable-length character string and varchar(n) is an equal-length character string.
fixed.w: Char(n) is padded to a fixed length n. varchar(n) stores up to n characters with variable length.

fixed.q: select name from instructor where dept_name = 'Physics' order by name; By default, the ORDER BY clause lists items in ____ order.
fixed.w: ORDER BY defaults to ASC.

fixed.q: Given relations R(w, x) and S(y, z), the result of SELECT DISTINCT w, x FROM R, S is guaranteed to be the same as R if
o: R has no duplicates and S is non-empty
R and S have no duplicates
S has no duplicates and R is non-empty
R and S have the same number of tuples
fixed.w: The cross product with a non-empty S repeats each R tuple, and DISTINCT collapses them back to R, but only if R had no duplicates (GATE 2000).

fixed.q: In an SQL query involving NOT, OR and AND without parentheses, what is the order of evaluation?
o: NOT followed by AND followed by OR
NOT followed by OR followed by AND
AND followed by OR followed by NOT
OR followed by AND followed by NOT
fixed.w: SQL precedence: NOT, then AND, then OR.

fixed.q: Which of the following statement is/are correct regarding sequential file organization? I. Entire file must be read for new record insertion and record deletion II. On an average, half of the records in the file must be processed to find the location of a record
fixed.w: In a sequential file, insertion or deletion needs the whole file to be rewritten, and on average n/2 records are read to find one. Both are true.

fixed.q: What is true about indexes?
o: Indexes improve performance even if the table is updated frequently.
It makes it harder for the SQL Server engine to work on indexes that have large keys.
It is not difficult for the SQL Server engine to work on indexes with large keys.
fixed.w: Wide (large) keys mean fewer entries per page and more I/O, so they are harder to work with. Frequent updates make indexes costlier, not faster.

fixed.q: A ____ index is one that satisfies all the columns requested in a query without performing a further lookup into the clustered index.
fixed.w: A covering index contains every column the query needs.

fixed.q: In RDBMS, B+ trees are preferred to binary trees since
o: Disk capacities are higher than memory capacities
Memory access is faster than disk access
Disks are more reliable than memory
fixed.w: B+ trees are shallow and wide, which minimises the number of slow disk accesses. Memory is far faster than disk.

fixed.q: Which of the following are steps in query processing?
fixed.w: Query processing has three steps: parse and translate, optimise, evaluate.

fixed.q:
Which of the following is a conflict serializable schedule?
S1: R1(A); R1(B); R2(A); R2(B); W2(B); W1(A)

S2: R1(A); R2(A); R2(B); W2(B); R1(B); W1(A)
o: S1 is conflict serializable but S2 is not.
S1 is not conflict serializable but S2 is conflict serializable.
fixed.w: S1: R1(B) before W2(B) gives T1→T2, and R2(A) before W1(A) gives T2→T1, a cycle, so S1 is not serializable. S2 has only T2→T1 edges, so it is conflict serializable.

fixed.q: Which of the following scenarios may lead to an irrecoverable error in a database system?
o: A transaction reads a data item after it is written by an uncommitted transaction.
A transaction writes a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction.
A transaction reads a data item after it is read by an uncommitted transaction.
A transaction reads a data item after it is written by a committed transaction.
fixed.w: Reading uncommitted data (a dirty read) creates an unrecoverable schedule if the reader commits and the writer then aborts (GATE 2003).

fixed.q: What is meant by the following relational algebra statement: STUDENT × COURSE?
o: Compute the cartesian product between the STUDENT and COURSE relations
Compute the natural join between the STUDENT and COURSE relations
Compute the left outer join between the STUDENT and COURSE relations

fixed.q: Which SQL command removes ALL rows but keeps the table structure and cannot be rolled back in most systems?
fixed.w: DELETE removes rows (DML, can use WHERE, can be rolled back); DROP removes the table itself.

fixed.q: Which of these is a DDL command?
fixed.w: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DCL: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.

fixed.q: Which clause filters GROUPS after aggregation?
fixed.w: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.

fixed.q: Which aggregate function ignores NULL values and counts only non-null entries in a column?
fixed.w: COUNT(*) counts all rows, including those with NULLs.

fixed.q: Which operator matches a pattern such as names starting with "A"?
fixed.w: % = any sequence of characters; _ = exactly one character.

fixed.q: BETWEEN 10 AND 20 in SQL is:
fixed.w: It equals >= 10 AND <= 20.

fixed.w: Any comparison with NULL using = gives UNKNOWN.

fixed.q: Which join returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right?
fixed.w: Unmatched right-side columns appear as NULL.

fixed.q: A CROSS JOIN of tables with 4 and 5 rows returns:
fixed.w: It is the Cartesian product.

fixed.q: Which constraint ensures a column value refers to an existing primary key in another table?
fixed.w: It enforces referential integrity.

o: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them
UNION works only on one table

o: Stores only the actual length used
fixed.w: CHAR is fixed length and padded with spaces.

fixed.q: In the three-schema architecture, the level that describes how data is physically stored is the:
fixed.w: External = user views; conceptual = logical structure of the whole database; internal = physical storage.

fixed.q: The ability to change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas is:
fixed.w: Physical independence = changing storage without changing the conceptual schema.

fixed.q: A repository of metadata (data about data) is the:
fixed.w: It holds table definitions, constraints and users.

fixed.q: The person with central control over the database and its users is the:
fixed.w: The DBA handles schema, security, backup and tuning.

theory.Basics:
• Data = raw facts; information = processed data. DBMS = software to store, retrieve and manage data safely (MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server — Microsoft).
• File-system problems a DBMS solves: redundancy & inconsistency, data isolation, integrity, atomicity, concurrent-access anomalies, security.
• Three levels (ANSI/SPARC): physical/internal (how stored), logical/conceptual (what is stored), view/external (what a user sees). Logical schema = organisation of information into parts.
• Physical data independence (easier): change internal schema without changing conceptual. Logical (harder): change conceptual without changing views/apps.
• Schema = design (rarely changes); instance = data at a moment.
• Catalog/data dictionary stores metadata.
• DBA: schema definition, storage & access methods, schema modification, authorisation, integrity constraints, maintenance.
• Query processor: DDL interpreter, DML compiler, embedded DML pre-compiler, query optimizer. Storage manager: authorization, integrity, transaction, file, buffer managers.
• Query processing: parsing & translation → optimisation → evaluation. Evaluation primitive = annotated RA operation; sequence = evaluation plan.
• Apps talk to DB via ODBC/JDBC. Design approaches: top-down, bottom-up, inside-out, mixed.
theory.ER model:
• Peter Chen, 1976; conceptual design.
• Symbols: rectangle = entity set; double rectangle = weak entity; ellipse = attribute; double ellipse = multivalued; dashed ellipse = derived; underline = key; dashed underline = discriminator; diamond = relationship; double diamond = identifying relationship; double line = total participation; arrow = 'one' side.
• Weak entity: no PK of its own; PK = owner PK + discriminator; total participation; many-to-one to owner.
• Degree: unary (recursive), binary (most common), ternary.
• Cardinality 1:1, 1:N, M:N. Modality 0 = optional, 1 = mandatory.
• Descriptive attributes describe relationships.
• ER → tables: M:N → separate table; 1:N → FK on N side; 1:1 → FK on either side (total side preferred); multivalued → separate table; composite → one column per part. Minimum tables: 1:1 total both sides 1, 1:N 2, M:N 3.
• Generalization bottom-up; specialization top-down (ISA); aggregation = relationship treated as entity.
• Connection traps: fan trap and chasm trap.
theory.Relational model:
• E. F. Codd, 1970; 12 rules for an RDBMS. Data in tables (relations).
• Tuple = row, attribute = column, domain = allowed atomic values. Degree (arity) = number of columns; cardinality = number of rows.
• Properties: atomic cells, unique rows, row order and column order don't matter.
theory.Keys:
• Super key: identifies tuples uniquely (X⁺ = all). Candidate key: minimal super key. Primary key: chosen candidate key, not NULL, one per table. Alternate key: other candidate keys. Composite key: several columns.
• Foreign key: refers to a primary key of another (or same) relation; table holding it = referencing relation, the other = referenced. Basis of referential integrity (FK matches a PK or is NULL).
• Entity integrity: PK can't be NULL. Domain, FD and referential constraints are special forms of an assertion.
• Prime attribute: part of some candidate key.
• Super keys with n attributes and single-attribute key: 2^(n−1). Two keys: inclusion–exclusion.
• Finding candidate keys: attributes never on any RHS must be in every key; grow from them until the closure covers all.
theory.Functional dependency:
• X → Y: equal X values imply equal Y values. Trivial if Y ⊆ X.
• Armstrong's axioms (sound & complete): reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity. Derived: union, decomposition, pseudo-transitivity (X→Y, WY→Z ⇒ WX→Z), composition.
• Closure X⁺: start with X, keep adding RHS of FDs whose LHS is inside. X⁺ = all → super key.
• F ≡ G iff F ⊆ G⁺ and G ⊆ F⁺. Canonical cover: single-attribute RHS, no extraneous LHS attributes, no redundant FDs.
theory.Normalization:
• Anomalies: insertion, update (modification), deletion. Fix by decomposition.
• 1NF: atomic values, no multivalued/composite attributes, no relations inside relations.
• 2NF: no partial dependency (non-prime depending on part of a candidate key). All single-attribute keys → automatically 2NF.
• 3NF: for every X → A, X is a super key OR A is prime (no transitive dependency).
• BCNF: every determinant X is a super key. Two-attribute relation always BCNF. All attributes prime → at least 3NF.
• 4NF: BCNF + no non-trivial MVD. 5NF: no join dependency.
• Lossless join (R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R2) is mandatory; dependency preservation desirable. 3NF can always have both; BCNF may lose dependencies.
• Finding the highest NF: find candidate keys and prime attributes, then test BCNF → 3NF → 2NF on each FD.
theory.File organisation:
• Ordered (sorted) file: binary search ⌈log₂ n⌉ block accesses; insert/delete costly. Heap (unordered): linear search (n/2 average), cheap inserts.
• Sequential file: insert/delete means rewriting the file; on average half the records read to find one.
• High volatility = frequent inserts/deletes. DASD = Direct Access Storage Device.
theory.Indexing:
• Index entry = key + block pointer; index files are sorted.
• Primary index: file ordered on primary key, one entry per block (sparse). Clustering index: file ordered on non-key, one entry per distinct value. Secondary index: unordered attribute, one entry per record (dense). At most one primary/clustering index, many secondary.
• Block accesses with a single-level index = ⌈log₂(index blocks)⌉ + 1. Blocking factor = ⌊B / record size⌋.
• Clustered index: rows physically sorted; one per table; default on the PRIMARY KEY in SQL Server. Covering index: has all columns the query needs. Large keys and frequent updates hurt index performance.
• B-tree order m: non-root node ⌈m/2⌉…m children, keys = children − 1, all leaves same level, data pointers in every node. Order: p·P + (p−1)(K + Pr) ≤ B.
• B+ tree: data pointers only in leaves; leaves linked (range queries); internal order p·P + (p−1)K ≤ B. Preferred because disk access is slow and high fan-out means few accesses.
• Hashing: best for equality search, poor for ranges.
theory.Relational algebra:
• Procedural; relational calculus is non-procedural. Foundation of SQL; set-based (no duplicates).
• Fundamental six: select σ (rows), project π (columns), rename ρ, union ∪, set difference −, Cartesian product ×. Derived: intersection (R − (R − S)), joins, division (for 'all' queries).
• Union/intersection/difference need union-compatibility (same arity and domains).
• Sizes: R × S → m·n tuples, degrees add. ∪: max(m,n)…m+n. ∩: 0…min(m,n). R − S: 0…m.
• Natural join: equal values on all common attributes, one copy each; no common attributes → Cartesian product. Outer joins keep unmatched tuples with NULLs (left, right, full).
theory.Relational calculus:
• TRC: {t | P(t)}, tuple variables. DRC: {⟨x1…xn⟩ | COND}, domain variables.
• Uses ∃, ∀, ∧, ∨, ¬. Safe expressions give finite results. Safe RC = RA in power (relationally complete).
theory.SQL:
• IBM System R, first called SEQUEL; standard SQL-86 (ANSI/ISO).
• DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT. DCL: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
• DELETE (DML, WHERE, can roll back) vs TRUNCATE (all rows, keeps table) vs DROP (removes table). ALTER TABLE … DROP CONSTRAINT. DROP SCHEMA … RESTRICT (only if empty) / CASCADE.
• SELECT * = all columns; DISTINCT removes duplicates (SQL keeps them by default); ORDER BY default ASC.
• Execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY. WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups (aggregates allowed only in HAVING).
• LIKE: % any string, _ exactly one character. Precedence NOT > AND > OR. BETWEEN inclusive; IS NULL, never = NULL.
• Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. All ignore NULLs except COUNT(*).
• Subqueries: > ALL = above max; < ALL = below min; > ANY/SOME = above min; = ANY = IN; EXISTS.
• Constraints: PRIMARY KEY (unique + not null), UNIQUE (allows NULL), NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT, FOREIGN KEY.
• CHAR(n) fixed, VARCHAR(n) variable. Concatenation ||. CEILING = smallest integer ≥ x. GETDATE() current timestamp (SQL Server); DATEDIFF(datepart, start, end) with datepart as a keyword.
• View = virtual table. Trigger = auto-run procedure on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (PL/SQL). Embedded SQL static; dynamic SQL built at run time.
theory.Transactions:
• ACID: atomicity (all or nothing — recovery), consistency (constraints/programmer), isolation (concurrency control), durability (committed changes persist — recovery).
• States: active → partially committed → committed; failed → aborted.
• Conflict: different transactions, same item, at least one write (RR never conflicts).
• Conflict serializable ⇔ precedence graph acyclic; serial order = topological sort. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable; view-only ones have blind writes.
• Recoverable: writer commits before reader commits. Cascadeless: read only committed data. Strict ⊆ cascadeless ⊆ recoverable. Reading uncommitted data and committing first → irrecoverable.
theory.Concurrency:
• Shared (S) lock: read, compatible with S. Exclusive (X): read/write, compatible with nothing.
• 2PL: growing then shrinking phase → conflict serializable, not deadlock-free. Strict 2PL: hold X locks till commit → recoverable, cascadeless. Rigorous: hold all locks. Conservative: lock all first → deadlock-free.
• Timestamp ordering: older TS first; read rejected if TS(Ti) < W-TS(Q); write rejected if TS(Ti) < R-TS or W-TS. Deadlock-free. Thomas write rule ignores obsolete writes.
• Deadlock: wait-for graph cycle. Wait-die: older waits, younger dies. Wound-wait: older wounds younger, younger waits.
• Intention locks IS, IX, SIX for multiple granularity; validation (optimistic) protocol: read, validate, write.
theory.Recovery:
• Log records: <Ti start>, <Ti, X, old, new>, <Ti commit>, <Ti abort>. Write-ahead logging: log before data.
• Deferred modification: writes at commit → redo only. Immediate: undo and redo.
• Checkpoints limit log scanning: redo committed after checkpoint, undo incomplete.
• Shadow paging: shadow page table kept; switch atomically at commit; no undo/redo.
